3 Amazing Things You’ll Only Find in South Korea 🇰🇷

DESCRIPTION

South Korea is known for its innovation, technology, and creative everyday solutions. In this video, we explore three unique things that make life in Korea different from many other countries around the world.

First, discover the frozen cup Matcha Latte experience. Instead of using ice that melts and waters down the drink, cafés use a cup that has been chilled in a freezer. Fresh milk and whisked matcha are poured directly into the frozen cup, keeping the drink cold and flavorful from the first sip to the very last.

Next, see a fully automatic hand-washing machine that takes hygiene to another level. This touch-free system dispenses soap, washes your hands, rinses them thoroughly, and even dries them automatically. It provides a convenient and efficient cleaning experience without requiring users to touch any surfaces.

Finally, learn about Korea's unmanned coin parking system. These compact parking areas use metal locking plates beneath vehicles. Once a car is parked, the plate rises to secure it in place. After payment is made at the machine, the plate lowers, allowing the driver to leave. It is a smart solution designed to maximize limited urban parking space.

Fast forward to 1979, the Iranian Revolution replaced the U.S.-backed Shah with Ayatollah Khomeini, and Iranian students stormed the U.S. Embassy, taking 52 Americans hostage for 444 days. This event marked the start of the modern era of hostility.

Since then, tensions have continued through sanctions, disputes over Iran’s nuclear program, and proxy conflicts in the Middle East. Attempts at diplomacy, including the 2015 nuclear deal, offered hope, but setbacks like the U.S. withdrawal in 2018 have kept relations strained.

What if everything you were taught about Africa was incomplete—or deliberately erased?

Long before slavery, colonization, and modern stereotypes, Africa was home to some of the greatest civilizations the world has ever known. From the Nile Valley and Nubia to Ghana, Axum, Kush, and beyond, Africa led the world in science, governance, architecture, trade, and education.

• What Africa really looked like before the fall

• And why remembering this past is essential for rebuilding the future

snippet.description:
Trace the history and evolution of beer, from its first known existence 13,000 years ago to the modern beverage we know today.

Today, there are over 100 distinct beer varieties, from pilsners and bocks, to porters, stouts, and IPAs. The oldest evidence of beer brewing dates back 13,000 years, but experts believe the drink developed independently across the world. So, how did ancient civilizations brew beer, and how did their methods develop into the beverage we know today? Malcolm Purinton traces the evolution of beer.

snippet.title: Ancient African Cosmology: Spiritual, Scientific, or Both?
snippet.description:
Ancient Africa has often been surrounded by mystery — but the real story is deeper than myths, aliens, or outside explanations.

In this documentary, we explore the hidden intelligence of African civilizations, from the Kingdom of Kongo and its layered spiritual worldview, to the rock art of Tassili n’Ajjer, the sky knowledge of the Dogon people, and the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela, Ethiopia.

This is not a story about proving fantasy. It is a journey into African history, ancient civilizations, spiritual cosmology, archaeology, astronomy, and the human imagination. Across the continent, African societies observed the heavens, built sacred architecture, preserved complex beliefs, and asked some of humanity’s oldest questions: Where do we come from? What is consciousness? And why have humans always looked to the sky for meaning?

Watch until the end, because the real mystery of ancient Africa was never whether beings came from the stars. The real mystery is how African civilizations developed such powerful systems of knowledge, memory, symbolism, and spiritual imagination.

Written and developed by the Legacy African History team. We use research, narration, editing, and modern AI-assisted visuals to bring African history to life with care, context, and respect.

Comment below: Do you think ancient sky stories were symbolic, observational, spiritual, or something more?

snippet.description:
One speech changed Africa forever. On June 30, 1960, Patrice Lumumba stood before kings, diplomats, and global cameras and did the unthinkable — he told the truth about colonialism. No weapons. No violence. Just words.

Six months later, he was dead.

This documentary reveals how the speech that got Patrice Lumumba killed exposed imperial power, terrified Western governments, and triggered one of the most chilling political assassinations of the Cold War. From Congo’s independence ceremony to secret meetings in Washington and Brussels, this is the story they tried to erase.

You won’t find this version in textbooks.

If you want to understand African decolonization, Cold War politics in Africa, and why Lumumba’s voice still echoes today, this film will change how you see history forever.

Watch to the end — because what happened after the speech is even more disturbing.

snippet.title: Mansa Musa: History's Richest Man Built on Slavery
snippet.description:
Updated upload — audio sync corrected.

Mansa Musa is history's richest man—a name synonymous with unimaginable gold and legendary wealth. But behind the dazzling stories of his 1324 pilgrimage that crashed Cairo's economy lies a far more complex and uncomfortable truth. The Mali Empire wasn't built on gold alone. It was built on systems of power, expansion, and human cost.

In this video, we explore the untold story of the Mali Empire—a civilization that stretched over a million square kilometers, patronized the scholars of Timbuktu, and created one of the most sophisticated societies of the medieval world. But we also confront the uncomfortable question: what fueled that golden machine?

From military campaigns against the Mossi, Songhai, and Fula kingdoms to the jonow laborers in the goldfields, from the tyeddo warrior-enforcers to the bustling markets of Timbuktu where manuscripts and human beings were traded streets apart—this is the full story. Not the myth. Not the meme. The empire in all its complexity.

We examine the trans-Saharan slave trade that Mali participated in—a stream compared to the tsunami of the trans-Atlantic trade that followed. We explore the indigenous legal codes that both protected scholars and codified ownership. We ask the hard questions: Can we hold both the gold and the dust in the same hand? Can we celebrate African greatness while acknowledging African complexity?

African history is world history. Not a sidebar of innocence, but a central chapter in the long, difficult story of human power. The libraries of Timbuktu exist because of Mali's strength—and that strength was forged, in part, in the crucible of capture.

To whitewash this history is to infantilize Africa. To tell the full story is to elevate it to the same demanding standard we apply to Rome, to Beijing, to London.
